macro_blurb: AI infrastructure and corporate restructuring dominate today's tape, with Anthropic topping CNBC's Disruptor 50 list and modular data center builder Armada raising $230 million alongside Johnson Controls to construct an Arizona factory, underscoring continued capex flows into US AI buildout. On the consumer side, Home Depot reported 5% sales growth and described its core shopper as resilient despite higher US gas prices, offering a constructive read on US home-improvement demand. In Europe, Standard Chartered announced 7,000 job cuts as it pivots toward AI, illustrating the cost-side impact of the same theme on European banking employment. German industrial news was heavier: battery maker Varta is closing its Nördlingen site after losing a major customer, a fresh signal of strain in Germany's EV-supply chain.
synthesis:
Today's screen is a pure US deep-value print: 10 of 10 picks are American, average Value percentile is 82.6 and average Yield 83.5, with composites ranging 71.3 to 100. Healthcare leads at 3 names, Financial Services at 2, and the rest scatter across Energy, Materials, Utilities, and Consumer. APA sweeps every factor at the 100th percentile — a 9.4x P/E, 11.9% FCF yield, 26% ROE and a 38% three-month return is a rare quadruple. The aggregate profile is cheap, cash-generative, and bought — not a quality screen, a value-and-yield screen with momentum confirmation.

Three threads hold the list together. First, an insurance/cash-return trade: ALL at 4.9x earnings with a $4B buyback, ACGL at 7.4x with an expanded repurchase — both top-quintile on Value and Quality, both telling you the underwriting cycle is being priced as peak. Second, a Healthcare value cluster — BIIB, CNC, BMY — surfacing against a sector down 13.6% over three months; CNC's 23.8% FCF yield comes with a -26% ROE, so the cheapness is doing real work. Third, AEP is the cleanest read on the macro: the Armada/Johnson Controls Arizona build and broader AI data-center capex give the utility a load-growth narrative, even as its -10% FCF yield flags the capex bill.

The outlier is MO — 5.75% yield, 80th-percentile momentum, but no reported ROE or book value, so it ranks on income and price action alone. The conspicuous absence is Technology and Industrials: zero picks from either, in a tape where AI infrastructure is the dominant capex story. That is the tension in this list — the screen is buying what AI isn't. Two things to watch over the next fortnight: any softening in oil that would unwind APA's quadruple, and follow-through on US consumer resilience (Home Depot's 5% print) that would either validate BBY's 6.6% yield or expose its -12.7% three-month drift.
